description: Negotiate by determining your Best Alternative To Negotiated Agreement before entering the room. Your BATNA is your walk-away power. Without it, you negotiate from fear. With it, you negotiate from strength.

steps.description: List every alternative to reaching a deal with this counterparty. What happens if you walk away?

inputs.name: negotiation-context
inputs.desc: What you are negotiating: the deal, the counterparty, what you want

inputs.name: current-situation
inputs.desc: Your current position if no deal is reached

outputs.name: alternatives-list
outputs.desc: Every alternative to this deal: other suppliers, other buyers, doing nothing, building in-house, waiting, or accepting the current situation

outputs.name: alternative-ranking
outputs.desc: Alternatives ranked by attractiveness: which is the best realistic option if this deal falls through

process: Sign up as a real customer, not a demo or trial (if possible). Use a real email, provide real information, and go through the same process any customer would.

Evaluate each alternative honestly. The best alternative is the one you would actually take, not the one that sounds best in a negotiation. If your real alternative is 'do nothing and suffer,' that is your BATNA.
Rank the alternatives by attractiveness. Your BATNA is the single best alternative. Everything below it is irrelevant; the BATNA is the floor below which you do not accept a deal.
Strengthen weak BATNAs before negotiating. If your best alternative is terrible, spend time improving it: get another offer, build a prototype, or develop a relationship with a competitor.

steps.description: Calculate your reservation price: the worst deal you would accept, because anything worse means you are better off taking your BATNA.

outputs.name: reservation-price
outputs.desc: The specific number, term, or condition below which you walk away. This is not a target; it is a floor.

outputs.name: walk-away-commitment
outputs.desc: The written commitment: if the deal goes below this point, you leave. Written before the negotiation to prevent emotional concession in the room.

process: Your reservation price is the value of your BATNA plus switching costs. If your BATNA is a competitor offering $90K, and switching to them costs $5K in time, your reservation price is $85K (net value).
Write the reservation price on paper before the negotiation. The purpose is to prevent yourself from making emotional concessions when the conversation gets difficult.
Never reveal your reservation price. It is internal. Revealing it gives the counterparty a target for their offer.

If your reservation price is very close to the counterparty's expected offer, the Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA) is narrow. Narrow ZOPAs require more creative deal structures to find value both parties can share.

steps.description: Estimate the counterparty's BATNA and reservation price. Their walk-away point determines how much you can push.

outputs.name: counterparty-batna-estimate
outputs.desc: Best guess at their alternatives: other customers, other suppliers, doing nothing, their status quo

outputs.name: counterparty-reservation-estimate
outputs.desc: Best guess at their floor: the worst deal they would accept before walking away

process: Research the counterparty's alternatives. Who else could they work with? What happens if they do nothing? Are they under time pressure?
Time pressure weakens a BATNA. If the counterparty has a deadline (budget expires, contract renews, board meeting), their BATNA degrades as the deadline approaches.
Multiple options strengthen a BATNA. If the counterparty has 5 other suppliers bidding, their BATNA is strong and you will need to differentiate on value, not just price.

The gap between your reservation price and their estimated reservation price is the ZOPA. If your floor is $85K and their estimated floor is $100K, the ZOPA is $85K-$100K. You want to capture as much of that gap as possible.

steps.description: Decide whether to make the first offer and what it should be, using anchoring theory.

outputs.name: first-offer-decision
outputs.desc: Whether to make the first offer (yes if you have good information about the ZOPA, no if you are uncertain about their valuation)

outputs.name: anchor-offer
outputs.desc: If making the first offer: the specific number, set aggressively but justifiably within the ZOPA

process: Make the first offer when you have good information about the ZOPA. The first offer anchors the negotiation: all subsequent offers are adjustments from this anchor.

Set the anchor aggressively but justifiably. If the ZOPA is $85K-$100K and you are selling, anchor at $110K with a justification (comparable deals, market rate, value delivered). The counterparty will negotiate down, but from your anchor.
Do not make the first offer when you have poor information. If you do not know the counterparty's BATNA, let them anchor first; their offer reveals information about their valuation.

Always justify the first offer. An anchor without justification feels arbitrary and provokes a negative reaction. An anchor with justification ('Based on comparable deals and the value delivered, the right number is $110K') feels like a data point.

steps.description: Plan your concessions in advance: each concession is smaller than the last, and each is traded for something in return.

outputs.name: concession-plan
outputs.desc: Pre-planned concessions: the first is the largest, each subsequent one is smaller, and each is conditional on receiving something in return

outputs.name: deal-structure
outputs.desc: The final deal terms including all trade-offs negotiated

process: Plan 3-4 concessions in advance, each smaller than the last. If the first concession is $10K, the second is $5K, the third is $2K. The decreasing size signals that you are approaching your limit.

Never concede without trading. Every concession you make should be paired with a request: 'I can do $100K if you can commit to a 2-year contract' or 'I can move on the price if we can accelerate the timeline.'
Avoid splitting the difference. It feels fair but leaves value on the table. Instead of 'let us meet in the middle,' trade on different dimensions: 'I will hold on price but give on payment terms.'
Close by summarizing the full deal, including all trade-offs. Both parties should feel they gave something and got something. If one party feels they lost, the deal is unstable.

description: Run a meeting that produces decisions, not discussion. Every meeting has one decision to make, the minimum people needed to make it, a pre-read, and a timer.

steps.description: Frame the single decision this meeting must make. If the meeting has no decision, cancel it.

inputs.name: context
inputs.desc: Background: why does this decision need to be made now

outputs.name: decision-statement
outputs.desc: The single decision in the form: 'We need to decide [specific choice] by [deadline] because [consequence of not deciding]'

outputs.name: decision-options
outputs.desc: The 2-4 options to choose between, each with pros/cons pre-documented

process: State the decision in one sentence: 'We need to decide whether to launch in Q1 or Q2.' If you cannot state the decision in one sentence, the meeting is not about a decision.
If the meeting has no decision (it is a status update, a brainstorm, or an FYI), cancel it. Status updates are emails. Brainstorms are documents. FYIs are Slack messages.
Document 2-4 options with pros and cons before the meeting. The meeting is for choosing between prepared options, not for discovering options in real time.
Every meeting must have a deadline consequence: 'We need to decide by Friday because engineering starts the sprint Monday.' Without urgency, decisions drift.

steps.description: Invite only the people who MUST be in the room for the decision. Everyone else gets the outcome in writing.

outputs.name: required-attendees
outputs.desc: The minimum set: the decision maker, the people with critical input, and no one else

outputs.name: informed-list
outputs.desc: People who need to know the outcome but do not need to be in the room

process: The decision maker must be in the room. If the decision maker is not available, cancel the meeting. A meeting without the decision maker produces discussion, not decisions.
Add people with critical input: those who have information the decision maker needs and cannot get from a document. Typically 2-4 people.
Everyone else goes on the informed list. They receive the decision and rationale after the meeting. This is not exclusion; it is respecting their time.
The maximum attendee count for a decision meeting is 7. Above 7, group dynamics prevent efficient discussion.

steps.description: Send a pre-read 24 hours before the meeting with the decision, options, and relevant data.

outputs.name: pre-read-document
outputs.desc: A 1-2 page document sent 24 hours before: the decision to make, the options with pros/cons, the relevant data, and the recommended option

outputs.name: preparation-request
outputs.desc: What each attendee should come prepared to discuss

process: Write the pre-read: one page maximum. Decision statement at the top, 2-4 options with pros/cons, relevant data, and your recommendation if you have one.
Send it 24 hours before the meeting with the expectation that attendees read it.
Include a recommendation if you have one. This is not pre-deciding; it gives the discussion a starting point.
Ask each attendee to come with their perspective on the options, not with new options. New options discovered in the meeting derail the decision.

steps.description: Run the meeting in 30 minutes or less: 5 minutes to confirm, 15 to discuss, 5 to decide, 5 for next steps.

outputs.name: decision-made
outputs.desc: The specific decision, stated clearly, with the rationale

outputs.name: next-steps
outputs.desc: Who does what by when as a result of the decision

outputs.name: meeting-record
outputs.desc: A 3-line record: the decision, the rationale, and the next steps with owners and deadlines

process: Open with 2 minutes confirming the decision and options. Do not re-explain the pre-read.
Run 15 minutes of focused discussion. Use a timer. When someone goes off-topic, redirect: 'That is interesting but not part of this decision. Can we take it offline?'
At the 20-minute mark, push for a decision. 'We have heard the discussion. What is the call?' If the decision maker needs more information, the meeting fails; schedule a follow-up.
Close with next steps in the last 5 minutes: who does what, by when. Read them aloud. Get verbal confirmation. Send the 3-line record within the hour.

description: Build a written argument using the Minto Pyramid: conclusion first, then supporting arguments, then evidence. The reader gets the answer in the first sentence, not the last.

steps.description: Write the conclusion first. The reader knows your answer in the first sentence.

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who will read this and what decision they need to make

outputs.name: conclusion-statement
outputs.desc: The one-sentence conclusion that answers the reader's question

outputs.name: reader-question
outputs.desc: The question the reader has that this document answers

process: Ask: what question does the reader have? 'Should we launch in Q1?' 'Is this project worth funding?' The conclusion is the answer to that question.
Write the conclusion as one sentence: 'We should launch in Q1 because the market window closes in March and the product is ready.' This is the first sentence of the document.
Do not build up to the conclusion. Academic writing builds argument, then concludes. Business writing concludes, then supports.
If you have multiple conclusions, you have multiple documents. Each document answers one question with one conclusion.

steps.description: Organize 2-4 supporting arguments under the conclusion, each answering 'why?' or 'how?'

inputs.name: reader-question
inputs.desc: What the reader needs to know

outputs.name: argument-structure
outputs.desc: 2-4 supporting arguments, each stated as a single sentence that directly supports the conclusion

outputs.name: argument-order
outputs.desc: Arguments ordered by importance or logical dependency

process: Each supporting argument answers 'why?' or 'how?' about the conclusion.
Limit to 2-4 arguments. More than 4 dilutes the strength of each.
Group arguments by type: inductive (evidence pointing the same direction) or deductive (if A and B then C).
Order matters: strongest first if reader might stop reading, logical order if arguments are dependent.

steps.description: Under each supporting argument, place evidence: data, examples, analogies, or expert opinions.

outputs.name: evidence-map
outputs.desc: Under each argument: 2-3 pieces of evidence that make the argument credible

outputs.name: evidence-gaps
outputs.desc: Arguments that lack strong evidence and need more research

process: For each argument, identify 2-3 pieces of evidence: data, examples, analogies, or authority.
Data is the strongest evidence. If data exists, use it. If not, say what you are relying on instead.
Flag evidence gaps. An argument without evidence is an assertion.
Two strong data points are better than five weak ones.

steps.description: Anticipate the reader's objections and address them before the reader raises them.

outputs.name: likely-objections
outputs.desc: The 2-3 objections the reader is most likely to raise

outputs.name: preemptive-responses
outputs.desc: For each objection: acknowledgment, response, and weakening evidence

process: Put yourself in the reader's position. Common objections: risk, cost, alternatives considered, evidence quality.
Address objections in the document, not in Q&A.
Acknowledging objections builds credibility. A document that ignores obvious risks looks naive.
If an objection is valid and not fully addressable, say so honestly.

steps.description: Assemble the final document: conclusion, supporting arguments with evidence, counter-arguments, and clear ask.

outputs.name: finished-document
outputs.desc: The complete document: conclusion first, arguments with evidence, objections addressed, specific ask at the end

outputs.name: executive-summary
outputs.desc: A 3-sentence version: conclusion, strongest evidence, ask

process: Assemble: First sentence is the conclusion. Next 2-4 sections are arguments with evidence. Then objections. End with a specific ask.
Write an executive summary: 3 sentences that give the reader everything if they read nothing else.
Cut ruthlessly. Every sentence must support the conclusion or address an objection.
The document should be readable in under 5 minutes. If longer, shorten it.

description: De-escalate a conflict by separating the person from the problem, acknowledging their emotions first, then moving to problem-solving.

steps.description: Acknowledge the other person's emotions before discussing the problem.

inputs.name: other-person-state
inputs.desc: How the other person seems to be feeling

outputs.name: acknowledgment-statement
outputs.desc: A statement that names and validates their emotion without agreeing with their position

outputs.name: emotional-temperature
outputs.desc: Assessment: is the person ready to problem-solve or do they need more acknowledgment?

process: Name the emotion you observe: 'You seem frustrated.' Naming an emotion reduces its intensity. Research shows that labeling emotions activates the prefrontal cortex and calms the amygdala.
Validate without agreeing: 'I understand why you would feel that way given what happened' does not mean 'You are right.' It means 'Your emotional response makes sense.'
Do not skip to problem-solving. Logic bounces off an activated emotional state.
Check the temperature: after acknowledging, does the person relax slightly? If yes, move to problem-solving. If no, continue acknowledging.

steps.description: Reframe from 'you vs me' to 'us vs the problem.'

outputs.name: reframed-problem
outputs.desc: The problem restated as a shared obstacle

outputs.name: shared-interest
outputs.desc: The interest both parties share that the problem threatens

process: Find the shared interest: what do both parties want? In most conflicts, both parties want something compatible.
Reframe: 'We both want this project to go well. The disagreement about the timeline is the obstacle. Let us figure it out together.'
The language matters: 'We' not 'you.' 'Us' not 'me.' 'Together' not 'you should.'
If the other person reverts to personal attacks, redirect: 'I hear your frustration. Let us focus on the problem.'

steps.description: Focus on interests (what each party needs) rather than positions (what each party demands).

outputs.name: interests-map
outputs.desc: Each party's underlying interests behind their stated positions

outputs.name: creative-options
outputs.desc: 3-5 options that serve both parties' interests

process: Distinguish positions from interests. A position is 'I want a raise.' The interest might be financial security, recognition, or career progression.
Ask: 'What is important to you about [their position]?' The answer reveals the interest.
Generate options that serve both interests.
Present 3-5 options and let the other party participate in choosing.

steps.description: Close with a specific agreement and repair the relationship.

outputs.name: resolution-agreement
outputs.desc: Who does what differently, by when, and the check-in date

outputs.name: relationship-repair
outputs.desc: A statement affirming the relationship

process: Make the agreement specific and time-bound.
Set a check-in: 'Let us revisit this in two weeks.'
Repair the relationship: 'I appreciate that we worked through this.'
Follow through immediately on whatever you committed to.

description: Persuade by asking questions, not by making arguments. Questions trigger the other person to convince themselves. Self-generated conclusions are stickier than imposed ones.

steps.description: Map what the other person currently believes and why.

inputs.name: persuasion-goal
inputs.desc: What you want the other person to believe, decide, or do

inputs.name: their-current-position
inputs.desc: What they currently believe and why

outputs.name: belief-map
outputs.desc: Their current belief, the evidence supporting it, and the emotional attachment to it

outputs.name: belief-gap
outputs.desc: The gap between their current belief and where you want them to go

process: Understand their belief fully before trying to change it.
Identify the type: factual, experiential, social, or identity-based. Each type requires a different approach.
Identity-based beliefs are the hardest to change through argument. Questions are the only effective approach.
Map the gap: what their evidence misses, not what yours adds.

steps.description: Design a sequence of questions that guides the person from their current belief to the conclusion you want them to reach on their own.

outputs.name: question-sequence
outputs.desc: 4-6 questions, each building on the previous answer, guiding toward the conclusion

outputs.name: anticipated-answers
outputs.desc: Expected answers and follow-up questions

process: Start with a question they will answer in a way that reveals a gap: 'What metrics are we using to measure whether the current approach is working?'
Each subsequent question builds on the previous answer and moves closer to the conclusion.
Never state the conclusion yourself. The final question should lead them to state it.
If they resist, ask: 'What am I missing?' Their answer reveals the real objection.

steps.description: Deliver the questions in conversation, adapting in real time.

outputs.name: conversation-record
outputs.desc: Your questions, their answers, and where they ended up

outputs.name: conclusion-reached
outputs.desc: The conclusion they arrived at in their own words

process: Ask questions with genuine curiosity, not as cross-examination.
Listen to each answer fully before asking the next question.
If they arrive at a different conclusion than expected, consider whether theirs is better.
If they arrive at your conclusion, let them own it.

steps.description: Help them commit to action and follow through on their self-generated conclusion.

outputs.name: action-commitment
outputs.desc: The specific action they commit to, stated in their own words

outputs.name: follow-up-plan
outputs.desc: When you will check in on progress

process: Ask: 'What is the first step you would take?' Self-generated first steps have higher follow-through.
Ask: 'When would you do that by?' A deadline makes it concrete.
Offer support, not direction: 'How can I help?' positions you as an ally.
Set a follow-up for accountability.

description: Write emails that get read and produce action: action requested first, context second, details last. Most emails fail because the ask is buried at the end.

steps.description: Write the subject line as a headline that tells the reader whether to open and what to do.

outputs.name: subject-line
outputs.desc: A subject line with action type and topic: 'Decision needed: Q1 launch date by Friday'

outputs.name: email-type
outputs.desc: action-required, decision-needed, FYI, or response-requested

process: Start the subject with the email type: 'Action needed:', 'Decision by [date]:', 'FYI:', or 'Response requested:'.
Include the topic and deadline in the subject.
Never use vague subjects: 'Quick question', 'Touching base', 'Update'.
If no action required, say so: 'FYI: No action needed.'

steps.description: Put the action or ask in the first line of the email body.

outputs.name: opening-line
outputs.desc: First sentence states exactly what you need

outputs.name: action-clarity
outputs.desc: The specific action, who does it, by when

process: First sentence = the ask. Everything else is context.
If multiple recipients with different actions, name them.
If FYI, the first line is the takeaway.
If responding to a question, the first line is the answer.

steps.description: Provide context in 2-3 sentences between the ask and the details.

outputs.name: context-block
outputs.desc: 2-3 sentences of context: why this matters, what led here, deadline pressures

outputs.name: context-sufficiency
outputs.desc: Whether the reader has enough context to act

process: Write 2-3 sentences of context, not a history.
Link to a document for complex context.
Include the consequence of not acting.
The context block should be skippable by readers who have context.

steps.description: Format details for scanning: bullets, bold, under 200 words total.

outputs.name: formatted-details
outputs.desc: Supporting details as bullet points with bold on key items

outputs.name: total-word-count
outputs.desc: Total email word count (target: under 200)

process: Use bullet points for any list of 3+ items.
Bold key items: deadlines, numbers, names of people who need to act.
Target 200 words total. Move details to attachment if longer.
End with a single clear next step.

description: Listen to understand, not to respond. Paraphrase, probe, and confirm before responding. Most people listen just long enough to formulate their reply.

steps.description: Set up conditions for full attention: eliminate distractions, signal you are listening.

inputs.name: conversation-context
inputs.desc: Who you are listening to and what the conversation is about

inputs.name: your-goal
inputs.desc: What you need to understand from this conversation

outputs.name: attention-plan
outputs.desc: Physical and mental setup for deep listening

outputs.name: listening-focus
outputs.desc: The specific information to extract

process: Remove distractions: phone face-down, laptop closed, notifications off.
Physical signals: face the speaker, maintain eye contact, nod occasionally.
Mental commitment: do not formulate your response while they are talking.
Set your listening focus: what do you need to learn?

steps.description: After they finish, paraphrase what you heard and confirm accuracy.

outputs.name: paraphrase-practice
outputs.desc: The habit of saying 'What I hear you saying is [their point]. Is that right?'

outputs.name: confirmation-record
outputs.desc: What they said, confirmed by them as accurate

process: After each major point, paraphrase: 'What I hear you saying is [restate in your words]. Is that accurate?'
If your paraphrase is wrong, their correction reveals the gap between said and understood.
Do not add interpretation to the paraphrase.
Paraphrasing slows the conversation, which is the point.

steps.description: Ask probing questions to go deeper into what they mean, feel, and need.

outputs.name: deeper-understanding
outputs.desc: Not just what they said, but what they meant and what they need

outputs.name: probe-questions-used
outputs.desc: The probing questions that produced deepest understanding

process: Ask 'What do you mean by [specific word]?' People use the same words for different things.
Ask 'How did that make you feel?' when emotions are involved.
Ask 'What would a good outcome look like for you?' to reveal their underlying interest.
Do not ask leading questions disguised as probes.

steps.description: Only after confirming full understanding do you respond with your own thoughts.

inputs.name: your-goal
inputs.desc: What you needed from the conversation

outputs.name: informed-response
outputs.desc: Your response informed by what you heard, acknowledging their points first

outputs.name: conversation-outcome
outputs.desc: What was agreed, decided, or learned

process: Start by referencing what they said: 'Based on what you described, here is how I see it.'
Address their points before making yours.
If your position changed based on what you heard, say so.
End with a summary of what was agreed or the next step.
